publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Factors Associated With Mental Health Outcomes Among Health Care Workers Exposed to Coronavirus Disease 2019

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the mental health of 1257 physicians and nurses in 34 Chinese hospitals with fever clinics or COVID-19 wards, surveyed over six days at the start of the outbreak
span.quote: This cross-sectional, survey-based, region-stratified study collected demographic data and mental health measurements from 1257 health care workers in 34 hospitals from January 29, 2020, to February 3, 2020, in China.

span.label: what is the magnitude of depression, anxiety, insomnia and distress among health care workers treating patients with COVID-19, and which occupational and geographic factors are associated with it
span.quote: To assess the magnitude of mental health outcomes and associated factors among health care workers treating patients exposed to COVID-19 in China.

span.label: a prevalence-and-risk-factor survey filling a gap the authors name: psychological assistance was already being deployed nationally while evidence-based evaluation of frontline workers was scarce
span.quote: However, evidence-based evaluations and mental health interventions targeting front-line health care workers are relatively scarce.

span.label: existence
span.quote: A considerable proportion of participants had symptoms of depression (634 \[50.4%\]), anxiety (560 \[44.6%\]), insomnia (427 \[34.0%\]), and distress (899 \[71.5%\]).

span.label: psychological burden in health care workers during an epidemic: 50.4% reported symptoms of depression, 44.6% anxiety, 34.0% insomnia and 71.5% distress
span.quote: A considerable proportion of participants had symptoms of depression (634 \[50.4%\]), anxiety (560 \[44.6%\]), insomnia (427 \[34.0%\]), and distress (899 \[71.5%\]).

span.label: region-stratified 2-stage cluster sampling of 34 hospitals, four validated Chinese instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, ISI, IES-R), nonparametric group comparisons and multivariable logistic regression
span.term: region-stratified 2-stage cluster sampling of 34 hospitals, four validated Chinese instruments (PHQ-9, GAD-7, ISI, IES-R), nonparametric group comparisons and multivariable logistic regression
span.quote: The study is a cross-sectional, hospital-based survey conducted via a region-stratified, 2-stage cluster sampling from January 29, 2020, to February 3, 2020. During this period, the total confirmed cases of COVID-19 exceeded 10 000 in China.

span.label: the authors' account of why frontline nurses fare worst - close, frequent contact and longer hours than usual, which is exposure to the hazard and exposure to the workload at once
span.quote: Frontline nurses treating patients with COVID-19 are likely exposed to the highest risk of infection because of their close, frequent contact with patients and working longer hours than usual.

span.label: human-to-human transmissibility and potential fatality are offered as intensifying the perception of personal danger - a belief about the disease rather than a dose of it
span.quote: The fact that COVID-19 is human-to-human transmissible,1, 3 associated with high morbidity, and potentially fatal16 may intensify the perception of personal danger.

span.label: predictable shortages of supplies together with rising case influx are named as contributors to pressure, separately from contact with patients
span.quote: Additionally, predictable shortages of supplies and an increasing influx of suspected and actual cases of COVID-19 contribute to the pressures and concerns of health care workers.17

span.label: 71.5% of nurses held junior titles, which the authors read as fewer years of work experience - offered as why the most exposed group is also the least practised
span.quote: Moreover, 71.5% of all nurses had junior titles, indicating that most had fewer years of work experience.

span.label: a list of distress sources taken from the SARS literature: vulnerability or loss of control, concern for self and family, changed work, isolation
span.quote: Sources of distress may include feelings of vulnerability or loss of control and concerns about health of self, spread of virus, health of family and others, changes in work, and being isolated.15

span.label: limited in scope - 81.2% of participants were from Hubei province, so the findings do not generalise to less affected regions
span.quote: First, it was limited in scope. Most participants (81.2%) were from Hubei province, limiting the generalization of our findings to less affected regions.

span.label: six days of collection and no longitudinal follow-up, so nothing here speaks to how the symptoms developed or resolved; the authors expect they worsened
span.quote: Second, the study was carried out during 6 days and lacks longitudinal follow-up. Because of the increasingly arduous situation, the mental health symptoms of health care workers could become more severe. Thus, long-term psychological implications of this population are worth further investigation.

span.label: NO COMPARATOR GROUP. The study cannot separate being a clinician in the region from living in the region, and cannot separate preexisting symptoms from new ones
span.quote: Third, this study was unable to distinguish the association of symptoms with being a clinician in this region vs simply living in this region (because there was no comparator group) and was also unable to distinguish preexisting mental health symptoms vs new symptoms.

span.label: response bias may remain at a 68.7% response rate, in either direction - the nonrespondents may have been too stressed to answer or not stressed enough to care
span.quote: Fourth, although the response rate of this study was 68.7%, response bias may still exist if the nonrespondents were either too stressed to respond or not at all stressed and therefore not interested in this survey.

span.label: the headline prevalences and the stated detection cutoffs are two different thresholds and the paper does not reconcile them in the abstract, where only the lower one appears
span.quote: A considerable proportion of participants had symptoms of depression (634 \[50.4%\]), anxiety (560 \[44.6%\]), insomnia (427 \[34.0%\]), and distress (899 \[71.5%\]).

span.label: multivariable logistic regression adjusting for sex, age, marital status, educational level, technical title, place of residence, working position and type of hospital
span.note: eliminates: the crude frontline-versus-second-line difference being an artefact of the front line's composition - sex, age, marital status, education, technical title, residence and hospital type are each held fixed, and those are the ones this quote names · outcome: held
span.quote: To determine potential risk factors for symptoms of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress in participants, multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed, and the associations between risk factors and outcomes are presented as odds ratios (ORs) and 95% CIs, after adjustment for confounders, including sex, age, marital status, educational level, technical title, place of residence, working position (first-line or second-line), and type of hospital.

span.label: all tests two-tailed at a significance level fixed in the Statistical Analysis section
span.note: eliminates: a one-tailed test chosen after the direction of an effect was already visible · outcome: held
span.quote: The significance level was set at α = .05, and all tests were 2-tailed.

span.label: nonparametric tests (Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis) after checking that none of the four score distributions was normal
span.note: eliminates: a normality assumption the data do not meet - the authors report the check and then choose the test that does not need it · outcome: held
span.quote: The original scores of the 4 measurement tools were not normally distributed and so are presented as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs). The ranked data, which were derived from the counts of each level for symptoms of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress, are presented as numbers and percentages. The nonparametric Mann-Whitney _U_ test and Kruskal-Wallis test were applied to compare the severity of each symptom between 2 or more groups.

span.label: four previously validated Chinese-language instruments with published band boundaries and cutoffs, rather than questions written for this study
span.note: eliminates: instrument novelty as the source of the prevalence figures, and makes the numbers comparable with other studies using the same scales · outcome: held
span.quote: We focused on symptoms of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress for all participants, using Chinese versions of validated measurement tools.

span.label: occupational and geographic data of the nonrespondents compared with those of respondents
span.note: eliminates: nonresponse being concentrated in one occupation or one region - but NOT response bias itself, which the authors say may still exist because the two things it would turn on, stress and interest, are exactly what was not measured in the people who declined · outcome: partial
span.quote: The occupational and geographic data of nonrespondents were similar to those of respondents (eTable 1 in the Supplement).

span.label: target sample size set from a stated formula, a stated margin of error and a 35% prior from the SARS literature, then amplified by 50% for subgroup analysis
span.note: eliminates: the subgroup comparisons being underpowered by accident - the amplification is declared in advance and for that purpose · outcome: held
span.quote: The target sample size of participants was determined using the formula N = Zα2P(1 − P) / d2, in which α = 0.05 and Zα = 1.96, and the estimated acceptable margin of error for proportion _d_ was 0.1. The proportion of health care workers with psychological comorbidities was estimated at 35%, based on a previous study of the SARS outbreak.7 To allow for subgroup analyses, we amplified the sample size by 50% with a goal of at least 1070 completed questionnaires from participants.

span.label: reporting followed the AAPOR guideline for survey research
span.note: eliminates: selective reporting of how the survey was conducted - a reporting standard is named in advance, which fixes the disclosures rather than leaving them to the authors' choice after the fact · outcome: held
span.quote: This study followed the American Association for Public Opinion Research ( AAPOR) reporting guideline.

span.label: a comparator group of people living in the same regions who were not clinicians
span.note: eliminates: living in the region rather than working in it as a clinician - the paper says plainly there was no comparator group, so the two cannot be separated · outcome: absent-declared-unreported · would have ruled out, had it been run: nothing - THE CONTROL WAS NOT AVAILABLE. The authors state they cannot separate being a clinician in this region from simply living in it, so the entire prevalence finding is uncontrolled against the background rate in Wuhan at the same moment
span.quote: Third, this study was unable to distinguish the association of symptoms with being a clinician in this region vs simply living in this region (because there was no comparator group) and was also unable to distinguish preexisting mental health symptoms vs new symptoms.

span.label: ethics committee approval, verbal informed consent, the right to terminate at any time, anonymity and assured confidentiality
span.note: eliminates: responses given under professional pressure during an outbreak being treated as freely given, when the respondents are staff of the reporting institution's own hospitals · outcome: held
span.quote: Approval from the clinical research ethics committee of Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University was received before the initiation of this study. Verbal informed consent was provided by all survey participants prior to their enrollment. Participants were allowed to terminate the survey at any time they desired. The survey was anonymous, and confidentiality of information was assured.

span.label: frontline workers
span.quote: Nurses, women, frontline workers, and those in Wuhan reported experiencing more severe symptom levels of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress

span.label: second-line workers
span.quote: Participants were asked whether they were directly engaged in clinical activities of diagnosing, treating, or providing nursing care to patients with elevated temperature or patients with confirmed COVID-19. Those who responded yes were defined as frontline workers, and those who answered no were defined as second-line workers.

span.label: nurses
span.quote: During the SARS outbreak, a study conducted among health care workers in emergency departments also showed that nurses were more likely to develop distress and use behavioral disengagement than physicians.15

span.label: physicians
span.quote: During the SARS outbreak, a study conducted among health care workers in emergency departments also showed that nurses were more likely to develop distress and use behavioral disengagement than physicians.15

span.label: COVID-19
span.quote: To assess the magnitude of mental health outcomes and associated factors among health care workers treating patients exposed to COVID-19 in China.

span.label: SARS
span.quote: In a previous study during the acute SARS outbreak, 89% of health care workers who were in high-risk situations reported psychological symptoms.8

span.label: Wuhan
span.quote: Working outside Hubei province was associated with a lower risk of feeling distressed than working in Wuhan (OR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.43-0.88; _P_ = .008).

span.label: Hubei province
span.quote: Working outside Hubei province was associated with a lower risk of feeling distressed than working in Wuhan (OR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.43-0.88; _P_ = .008).

span.label: tertiary hospital
span.quote: Compared with working in a tertiary hospital, working in secondary hospitals was associated with more severe symptoms of depression (OR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.17-2.34; _P_ = .004) and anxiety (OR, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.08-1.90; _P_ = .01).

span.label: secondary hospitals
span.quote: Compared with working in a tertiary hospital, working in secondary hospitals was associated with more severe symptoms of depression (OR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.17-2.34; _P_ = .004) and anxiety (OR, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.08-1.90; _P_ = .01).

span.quote: Second, the study was carried out during 6 days and lacks longitudinal follow-up. Because of the increasingly arduous situation, the mental health symptoms of health care workers could become more severe. Thus, long-term psychological implications of this population are worth further investigation.

span.label: symptoms of depression / anxiety / insomnia / distress, AS USED IN THE FOUR HEADLINE PREVALENCES - a count of everyone scoring above NORMAL on each scale, which is a far lower bar than the cutoff the same paper defines for detecting each disorder. Read this figure with the band boundaries tagged under definitions and with the two statistics rows that quote Table 2's own band counts; the number is right and the sense is milder than the words suggest
span.quote: A considerable proportion of participants had symptoms of depression (634 \[50.4%\]), anxiety (560 \[44.6%\]), insomnia (427 \[34.0%\]), and distress (899 \[71.5%\]).

span.label: severe symptoms - A SECOND AND HIGHER THRESHOLD IN THE SAME PAPER: a score greater than 10, 7, 15 or 26. For distress that cutoff of 26 falls at the boundary of the moderate band, while the 71.5% headline counts from the mild band up. SO `distress' IN THIS PAPER NAMES TWO DIFFERENT POPULATIONS DEPENDING ON WHICH SENTENCE YOU READ, and both are correct
span.quote: The cutoff score for detecting symptoms of major depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress were 10, 7,14 15, and 26, respectively. Participants who had scores greater than the cutoff threshold were characterized as having severe symptoms.

span.label: distress - A SCORE ON THE IMPACT OF EVENT SCALE-REVISED, an instrument for the psychological impact of a specific event, not a clinical diagnosis and not general unhappiness. The same instrument carries the same sense in wang2020, where the label is `psychological impact` instead
span.quote: Accordingly, the 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9; range, 0-27),10 the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) scale (range, 0-21),11 the 7-item Insomnia Severity Index (ISI; range, 0-28),12 and the 22-item Impact of Event Scale–Revised (IES-R; range, 0-88)13 were used to assess the severity of symptoms of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress, respectively.

span.label: frontline - SELF-REPORTED AND BINARY. It is a yes/no answer to whether the respondent was directly engaged in diagnosing, treating or nursing patients with fever or confirmed COVID-19; it carries no measure of hours, caseload or duration of exposure
span.quote: Participants were asked whether they were directly engaged in clinical activities of diagnosing, treating, or providing nursing care to patients with elevated temperature or patients with confirmed COVID-19. Those who responded yes were defined as frontline workers, and those who answered no were defined as second-line workers.

span.label: risk factor / associated with - AN ADJUSTED CROSS-SECTIONAL ODDS RATIO. Confounders are named and controlled, which is more than wang2020's univariate analysis does, but the design still observes no temporal order: nobody was measured before becoming frontline
span.quote: To determine potential risk factors for symptoms of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress in participants, multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed, and the associations between risk factors and outcomes are presented as odds ratios (ORs) and 95% CIs, after adjustment for confounders, including sex, age, marital status, educational level, technical title, place of residence, working position (first-line or second-line), and type of hospital.

span.label: builds-on → the SARS-outbreak literature on health care workers (Maunder 2003, Bai 2004, Lee 2007, Chua 2004), which reported 89% with psychological symptoms in high-risk situations
span.quote: In a previous study during the acute SARS outbreak, 89% of health care workers who were in high-risk situations reported psychological symptoms.8

span.label: confirms → the SARS emergency-department finding that nurses developed more distress and more behavioural disengagement than physicians
span.note: the paper's own word is `also showed`, which is agreement reported after the fact and not a replication attempt - `confirms` rather than `replicates` for that reason
span.quote: During the SARS outbreak, a study conducted among health care workers in emergency departments also showed that nurses were more likely to develop distress and use behavioral disengagement than physicians.15

span.label: qualifies → the national deployment of psychological assistance hotlines and counselling during the outbreak, which this paper says ran ahead of any evidence base for frontline workers
span.quote: Psychological assistance services, including telephone-, internet-, and application-based counseling or intervention, have been widely deployed by local and national mental health institutions in response to the COVID-19 outbreak. On February 2, 2020, the State Council of China announced that it was setting up nationwide psychological assistance hotlines to help during the epidemic situation.9 However, evidence-based evaluations and mental health interventions targeting front-line health care workers are relatively scarce.

span.label: frontline workers —causes→ insomnia
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.85 — the paper's word is `independent risk factor`, which is an adjusted cross-sectional association and not a demonstrated cause; the weight is below 1.0 for that reason and the largest of the four odds ratios is this one
span.quote: Compared with working in second-line positions, working in the frontline directly treating patients with COVID-19 appeared to be an independent risk factor for all psychiatric symptoms after adjustment (depression, OR 1.52; 95% CI, 1.11-2.09; _P_ = .01; anxiety, OR 1.57; 95% CI, 1.22-2.02; _P_ < .001; insomnia, OR 2.97; 95% CI, 1.92-4.60; _P_ < .001; distress: OR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.25-2.04; _P_ < .001)

span.quote: A considerable proportion of participants had symptoms of depression (634 \[50.4%\]), anxiety (560 \[44.6%\]), insomnia (427 \[34.0%\]), and distress (899 \[71.5%\]).

span.label: frontline work was an independent risk factor for all four outcomes after adjustment; insomnia carried much the largest odds ratio at 2.97
span.quote: Compared with working in second-line positions, working in the frontline directly treating patients with COVID-19 appeared to be an independent risk factor for all psychiatric symptoms after adjustment (depression, OR 1.52; 95% CI, 1.11-2.09; _P_ = .01; anxiety, OR 1.57; 95% CI, 1.22-2.02; _P_ < .001; insomnia, OR 2.97; 95% CI, 1.92-4.60; _P_ < .001; distress: OR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.25-2.04; _P_ < .001)

span.label: being a woman and holding an intermediate professional title were associated with severe depression, anxiety and distress
span.quote: Multivariable logistic regression analysis showed that, after controlling for confounders, being a woman and having an intermediate professional title were associated with severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and distress (eg, severe depression among women: OR, 1.94; 95% CI, 1.26-2.98; _P_ = .003; severe anxiety among those with intermediate professional titles: OR, 1.82; 95% CI, 1.38-2.39; _P_ < .001).

span.label: working outside Hubei province carried a LOWER risk of distress than working in Wuhan - the only protective association in the model
span.quote: Working outside Hubei province was associated with a lower risk of feeling distressed than working in Wuhan (OR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.43-0.88; _P_ = .008).

span.label: secondary-hospital staff reported more severe depression and anxiety than tertiary-hospital staff
span.quote: Compared with working in a tertiary hospital, working in secondary hospitals was associated with more severe symptoms of depression (OR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.17-2.34; _P_ = .004) and anxiety (OR, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.08-1.90; _P_ = .01).

span.label: but frontline workers in secondary and tertiary hospitals scored equally high on all four scales - the hospital-type difference disappears at the front line
span.quote: However, frontline health care workers from tertiary and secondary hospitals reported equally high scores on all 4 scales (eg, median \[IQR\] PHQ-9 score, 5.0 \[2.0-8.0\] vs 6.0 \[3.0-9.0\]; _P_ = .08) ( Table 4).

span.label: nurses, women, frontline workers and those in Wuhan reported more severe symptoms on every measurement
span.quote: Nurses, women, frontline workers, and those in Wuhan reported experiencing more severe symptom levels of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress

span.label: frontline worker = answered yes to being directly engaged in diagnosing, treating or nursing patients with fever or confirmed COVID-19; everyone else is second-line
span.quote: Participants were asked whether they were directly engaged in clinical activities of diagnosing, treating, or providing nursing care to patients with elevated temperature or patients with confirmed COVID-19. Those who responded yes were defined as frontline workers, and those who answered no were defined as second-line workers.

span.label: band boundaries for all four scales, from PHQ-9 normal 0-4 through IES-R severe 44-88
span.quote: The total scores of these measurement tools were interpreted as follows: PHQ-9, normal (0-4), mild (5-9), moderate (10-14), and severe (15-21) depression; GAD-7, normal (0-4), mild (5-9), moderate (10-14), and severe (15-21) anxiety; ISI, normal (0-7), subthreshold (8-14), moderate (15-21), and severe (22-28) insomnia; and IES-R, normal (0-8), mild (9-25), moderate (26-43), and severe (44-88) distress.

span.label: cutoffs for detecting major depression, anxiety, insomnia and distress: 10, 7, 15 and 26; above the cutoff is called severe
span.quote: The cutoff score for detecting symptoms of major depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress were 10, 7,14 15, and 26, respectively. Participants who had scores greater than the cutoff threshold were characterized as having severe symptoms.

span.label: the four instruments and their ranges: PHQ-9 0-27, GAD-7 0-21, ISI 0-28, IES-R 0-88
span.quote: Accordingly, the 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9; range, 0-27),10 the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) scale (range, 0-21),11 the 7-item Insomnia Severity Index (ISI; range, 0-28),12 and the 22-item Impact of Event Scale–Revised (IES-R; range, 0-88)13 were used to assess the severity of symptoms of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress, respectively.

span.label: 1257 of 1830 contacted individuals completed the survey, a participation rate of 68.7%
span.quote: A total of 1257 of 1830 contacted individuals completed the survey, with a participation rate of 68.7%.

span.label: 1257 health care workers in 34 hospitals, over six days from 29 January to 3 February 2020
span.quote: This cross-sectional, survey-based, region-stratified study collected demographic data and mental health measurements from 1257 health care workers in 34 hospitals from January 29, 2020, to February 3, 2020, in China.

span.label: 20 hospitals in Wuhan, 7 elsewhere in Hubei, 7 in other provinces - 34 in total
span.quote: A total of 20 hospitals in Wuhan (10 designated by the local government to treat COVID-19 and 10 nondesignated), 7 hospitals in other regions of Hubei province, and 7 hospitals from 7 other provinces with a high incidence of COVID-19 (1 hospital from each province) were included. In total, 34 hospitals were involved.

span.label: median scores: PHQ-9 5.0, GAD-7 4.0, ISI 5.0, IES-R 20.0
span.quote: The median (IQR) scores on the PHQ-9 for depression, the GAD-7 for anxiety, the ISI for insomnia, and the IES-R for distress for all respondents were 5.0 (2.0-8.0), 4.0 (1.0-7.0), 5.0 (2.0-9.0), and 20.0 (7.0-31.0), respectively.

span.label: target sample of at least 1070 completed questionnaires, from a 35% prior and a 50% amplification for subgroups
span.quote: The target sample size of participants was determined using the formula N = Zα2P(1 − P) / d2, in which α = 0.05 and Zα = 1.96, and the estimated acceptable margin of error for proportion _d_ was 0.1. The proportion of health care workers with psychological comorbidities was estimated at 35%, based on a previous study of the SARS outbreak.7 To allow for subgroup analyses, we amplified the sample size by 50% with a goal of at least 1070 completed questionnaires from participants.

span.label: frontline vs second-line, adjusted: depression OR 1.52 (1.11-2.09), anxiety 1.57 (1.22-2.02), insomnia 2.97 (1.92-4.60), distress 1.60 (1.25-2.04)
span.quote: Compared with working in second-line positions, working in the frontline directly treating patients with COVID-19 appeared to be an independent risk factor for all psychiatric symptoms after adjustment (depression, OR 1.52; 95% CI, 1.11-2.09; _P_ = .01; anxiety, OR 1.57; 95% CI, 1.22-2.02; _P_ < .001; insomnia, OR 2.97; 95% CI, 1.92-4.60; _P_ < .001; distress: OR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.25-2.04; _P_ < .001)

span.label: outside Hubei vs Wuhan, distress OR 0.62 (0.43-0.88), P = .008
span.quote: Working outside Hubei province was associated with a lower risk of feeling distressed than working in Wuhan (OR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.43-0.88; _P_ = .008).

span.label: secondary vs tertiary hospital: depression OR 1.65 (1.17-2.34), anxiety OR 1.43 (1.08-1.90)
span.quote: Compared with working in a tertiary hospital, working in secondary hospitals was associated with more severe symptoms of depression (OR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.17-2.34; _P_ = .004) and anxiety (OR, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.08-1.90; _P_ = .01).

span.label: severe depression among women OR 1.94 (1.26-2.98); severe anxiety with an intermediate title OR 1.82 (1.38-2.39)
span.quote: Multivariable logistic regression analysis showed that, after controlling for confounders, being a woman and having an intermediate professional title were associated with severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and distress (eg, severe depression among women: OR, 1.94; 95% CI, 1.26-2.98; _P_ = .003; severe anxiety among those with intermediate professional titles: OR, 1.82; 95% CI, 1.38-2.39; _P_ < .001).

span.label: THE 71.5% DISTRESS FIGURE IS EVERY IES-R BAND ABOVE NORMAL: 459 mild + 308 moderate + 132 severe = 899 of 1257. The severe band alone is 132, or 10.5%, and the paper's own stated cutoff for detecting distress is 26 - the boundary of the moderate band, not of the mild one
the same shape on the PHQ-9: 448 mild + 108 moderate + 78 severe = 634 of 1257 = the reported 50.4%, while the stated cutoff for detecting major depression is 10
all tests 2-tailed with the significance level fixed in advance; group comparisons by Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis because none of the four distributions was normal
span.quote: The original scores of the 4 measurement tools were not normally distributed and so are presented as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs). The ranked data, which were derived from the counts of each level for symptoms of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress, are presented as numbers and percentages. The nonparametric Mann-Whitney _U_ test and Kruskal-Wallis test were applied to compare the severity of each symptom between 2 or more groups.
